post_text:
A green dashboard can lie to you with absolute confidence.

Three years ago, I refused to rely on our gateway's aggregate HTTP 200 success metrics.

Instead, I added boring JVM-level Micrometer gauges tracking empty partial payloads and executor queue wait times.

The team pushed back, calling it redundant boilerplate when the ingress proxies already tracked automated telemetry.

I doubted myself for weeks, wondering if my lingering anxiety was just slowing down feature delivery.

Nine months later, a downstream database migration degraded, causing workers to catch timeouts and return empty response envelopes with HTTP 200 OK.

The company-wide latency dashboards stayed pristine, but my obscure payload-anomaly alert fired quietly at 2 AM before customers noticed missing transactions.

We patched the fallback handler before the morning rush without incident.

There were no heroic escalations or dramatic war rooms. I was just quietly relieved that our internal health checks monitored the actual state of data rather than an arbitrary protocol code.

What I learned:

Aggregate success metrics often measure whether a server replied, not whether it actually did the work.
